conventions.convention: A well-order is a total order with a least element in every nonempty subset. Its strict presentation is irreflexive, transitive and trichotomous. The empty set is well ordered.
An order embedding preserves and reflects the weak order; an order isomorphism is a surjective embedding. A strictly increasing bijection between total orders is an order isomorphism.
Initial segments are downward closed and include the whole well-order and the empty set. Every proper initial segment is W_<a for exactly one a.

Transfinite recursion is a ZF theorem schema for a formula-defined, set-valued class function total on every function whose domain is a proper initial segment of the supplied set well-order. No Choice is assumed.
An ordinal is a transitive set strictly well ordered by membership. For ordinals, α<β means α∈β, and α⁺ means α∪{α}. Foundation is not required for the ordinal proofs using this definition.
Zero is excluded from limit ordinals. A limit ordinal is a nonzero ordinal that is not a successor.
The Hartogs number is the least ordinal admitting no injection into A, and equals the set of order types of all well-orders of subsets of A.
Being a cardinal is a choice-free property of an ordinal. The assignment |X| to arbitrary sets is defined under AC as the least ordinal equinumerous with X.
In the explicit integer well-order, absolute value is compared first and the positive integer precedes the negative integer at equal nonzero absolute value.
The integer collapsing-recursion counterexample works in ZF with Foundation; its descending-value sequence is indexed from n=0 with x_n=F(-(n+1)).

load_bearing.statement: For ordinals α and β: every element of α is an ordinal; α∉α; α⁺ is an ordinal; the intersection of a nonempty set of ordinals is an ordinal; the union of any set of ordinals is an ordinal; α⊆β iff α∈β or α=β; and any two ordinals are comparable under inclusion. No choice principle is used.

For ordinals α and β, exactly one of α∈β, α=β, β∈α holds. Every nonempty set of ordinals has an ∈-least element; every set of ordinals is well ordered by inclusion, whose strict part is membership. No choice principle is used.

Let (W,<) be a well-order and G a formula-defined class function assigning a set G(h) to every function h whose domain is a proper initial segment of W. There is exactly one function F with domain W satisfying F(a)=G(F restricted to W_<a) for every a∈W. This is a theorem schema of ZF using Replacement and no Choice.
Every well-order (W,<) is order isomorphic to exactly one ordinal, its order type. The unique isomorphism is the collapsing map F(a)={F(b):b<a}. This uses Replacement and no Choice.
For every set A there is an ordinal that does not inject into A. The least such ordinal, ℵ(A), equals {ot(S,R):S⊆A and R well-orders S}. The proof is choice free.

For a well-order W and strictly increasing f:W→W, a≤f(a) for every a∈W. W is not order isomorphic to any proper initial segment of itself; its only order automorphism is the identity; and between any two well-orders there is at most one order isomorphism. No Choice is used.
For well-orders V and W, exactly one holds: V≅W; V≅W_<b for a unique b∈W; or V_<a≅W for a unique a∈V. No choice principle is used.

For von Neumann naturals m,n, m∈n iff m<n. Every natural number and ω are ordinals; ω is a limit ordinal; every ordinal in ω is zero or a successor; and ω⊆γ for every limit ordinal γ. No Choice is used.
Let (W,<) be a well-order and S⊆W. If, for every a∈W, W_<a⊆S implies a∈S, then S=W. This is a theorem of ZF using no Choice.
Over ZF, the Axiom of Choice, Zorn's lemma, and the assertion that every set can be well ordered are equivalent.

concerns.concern: The order-type remark says the equivalence class of the empty well-order is the singleton {∅}. Under def-well-order, a well-order is the pair (W,≤), so this class is {(∅,∅)}, rather than {∅}. The proper-class comparison remains correct, but the singleton description needs to identify its coding convention.

The uniqueness remark says: 'A construction phrased as "at stage a pick some element not yet used" is a different theorem and does cost a choice principle.' This needs an 'in general' qualification: finite successive selections require no choice axiom, and a supplied well-order can determine unused elements canonically. The stated recursion theorem and its proof are unaffected.

The 'useful test' says that when the answer is 'some element with the following property' and there is generally more than one candidate, 'a choice function is being used and must be paid for.' Multiple candidates and informal selection language alone do not establish a choice-axiom cost: finite selections or a supplied canonical selector are choice-free. Qualify this heuristic consistently with the item's distinction between supplied data and unavailable selectors.
